To Spear a Fish

  • BY Theodore R. Niekras
  • August 20, 2026

Eat

Photography by Luke Schmuecker

Photography by Luke Schmuecker

Photography by Luke Schmuecker

PRINT

The ancient fishing practice the comes with risks and rewards

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:41
Instaread

Mitsuki Hara was once a new international student from Japan at UC San Diego. When she first arrived in San Diego, she didn’t have many friends, family, or money. It was tough. She grew up rod and reel fishing with her family, so she would often fish along the coast of La Jolla.

One day while fishing, she saw something that piqued her interest … and her appetite.

“I saw these guys come out from the water with lobsters. That kind of gave me an idea. Like, oh, maybe I want to try this out because I like lobster, but I can’t afford it,” she tells me.

There was a problem: Hara was deathly afraid of deep water because of a near-drowning as a child. Something, though—maybe the idea of eating fresh and free lobster—drove her to face this fear.

“I had this buoy with a metal chain on the bottom, that’s maybe like 10 or 11, like 15 feet or less than that. I tried it once, going down to the bottom using that line, and I realized that it wasn’t scary at all.”

In fact, it was beautiful.

Shortly after, Hara went to a meetup with the San Diego Freedivers, a freediving and spearfishing community. They welcomed her, mentored her, and taught her to spearfish.

From then on—excuse the pun—she was hooked. Years later, Hara is now a two-time world record holder and still goes out to spear seasonal fish to eat regularly.

The same can be said of Spear America San Diego owner Ryan Moore. He grew up in Los Angeles and now owns one of the nation’s largest freediving and spearfishing shops in the US. Moore has also traveled the world spearfishing and is on the board of the San Diego Freedivers.

He went rod and reel fishing as a child, but her never really took to it.

As a teenager, though, Moore got a mask, snorkel, and fin set from Costco, used an old wetsuit, and found a friend with a speargun. “It was a lot more dynamic,” he tells me. “You were hunting, you were swimming around, you were seeing all the wildlife in its habitat, and I was immediately hooked. In fact, since the first day I went spearfishing, I haven’t gone a single day of my life without thinking about it all day.”

For many “spearos” like these two, there’s a multitude of factors that brought them to the point of obsession. There’s the connection with nature, the meditative aspect of underwater breath-holding. There’s also the competition and community. Most of all, it is the personal connection to the fish they will hunt and eat.

“Gathering your own food is something that so many people have lost touch with. Today, you go to the market and food comes prepackaged, and it doesn’t look like the animal it started out as,” Moore tells me. “What draws me to spearfishing is I’m all about going out and collecting my own food and teaching other people to do that as well.”

Spearfishing has seen an explosion in global popularity in the last decade, with San Diego being one of many hotbeds for the sport due to its long fishing heritage and productive waters.

Historically, using a spear to fish is one of the oldest forms of fishing, dating back at least 16,000 years. Ancient cave art in France depicts humans spearing fish. Literature from ancient Greece details methods and techniques. In Rome, it was a recreational pastime of the elite. Various island cultures, most notably the Polynesians, traditionally speared fish.

As it turns out, San Diego’s spearfishing heritage goes back millennia.

Richard Carrico, a professor in the Department of American Indian Studies at San Diego State University, has extensively dug archeological sites all over San Diego. What he found in archeological digs over 20 years was archaeological and anthropological evidence of the San Diego Kumeyaay’s own spearing heritage.

Traditionally thought to have subsisted mostly on inland resources, Carrico found the Kumeyaay were utilizing San Diego’s productive coastline to sustain populations far larger than inland food sources like deer, acorn, and rabbit could sustain.

“Archeologically, at a couple of the sites in Sorrento Valley, there was a village called East Owa that we dug that went back more than 2,000 years,” Carrico explained. “And in Sorrento Valley, we found 32 species of fish.”

“There was another huge, huge site on Ballast Point down there, near Point Loma,” he continued. “Especially there at Ballast Point, we found what I would believe, and my other colleague Dennis Gallegos, are barbed spear points.”

These spear points, he explained, were usually tied with sinew to willow or arrowwood poles, and, judging by the bones they excavated, were used to spear many species then found in the bay.

More recently, modern spearfishing got its start in the United States in La Jolla, when a group of freedivers formed the San Diego Bottom Scratchers in 1933. With homemade masks, they dove the chilly waters of La Jolla Cove without wetsuits, using tridents to spear 200-pound fish.

Spearfishing has evolved over time, but it remains true to its ancient roots as a practical, economical, and effective way to target fish to eat.

Moore notes that it’s accessible and can be done without the excessive price tag of a sportfishing charter. Although you can spend about $1,000 on a medium-quality kit that comes with all you need, you don’t have to. Like Moore, a mask and fins from Costco, a fishing license, and a borrowed speargun or pole spear will work. With the closure of Ocean Beach Pier, there are few options left for the public to fish species of kelp fish without having to charter a boat. Spearfishing helps fill that space.

“You could just swim off the beach here almost any day of the year and capture calico or halibut,” Moore says. “So many of our local fish, I think, are 100 times better than those other options you buy in the market.”

Importantly, though, the sport is not without its dangers. Shallow water blackouts, where you pass out coming to the surface, can be fatal. Hara has had two; she was also once shot in the leg with a spear. That’s why it’s best to join a club or learn from those more experienced.

“You have to really listen to us, really understand what we do,” Hara warns. “It’s a dangerous sport.”

For those willing to try, it offers something remarkable: the chance to put the freshest and most sustainably caught fish directly on the table. To be out in nature. To connect with food in a way that most people never get a chance to experience in our modern world.

DISCLAIMER: Safety & Liability
The information provided in this article is intended for educational and informational purposes only. Ocean spearfishing is an inherently dangerous activity that carries significant risks, including but not limited to drowning, shallow water blackouts, marine animal encounters, equipment failure, strong currents, and other life-threatening hazards.

By reading and applying any information contained in this article, you acknowledge and agree that:

1. You assume full and sole responsibility for your own safety and the safety of others in your party.

2. You will obtain proper training, certification, and supervision from qualified instructors before engaging in spearfishing activities.

3. You will comply with all applicable federal, state, and local laws, regulations, and licensing requirements governing spearfishing in your jurisdiction.

4. You will never spearfish alone and will always dive with a qualified buddy or certified dive professional.

5. You will assess your own physical fitness, skill level, and environmental conditions before entering the water.

Theodore R. Niekras

Theodore R. Niekras sails, surfs, spears, and cooks in San Diego, among other places. He holds a master’s in creative writing from San Diego State University. His interests include foraging, good food journalism, and being close to nature.
